title: String Matching in an Array
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every pair of words versus sorting by length to skip impossible comparisons.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of strings words, return every string in it that is a substring of some other string in the same array.

It helps to ask which pairwise comparisons are guaranteed to fail before a single character is even checked.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force compares every word against every other word in both directions, but a word can never be a substring of another word that is the same length or shorter, so a large share of these comparisons are doomed from the start.

Observation 2: Three Sum already showed that sorting by a simple, cheap to compute property before doing the more expensive per-pair work eliminates a whole class of guaranteed failures up front.

Observation 3: Here that cheap property is simply string length; sorting all words by length once means every word only ever needs to be checked against words later in that order, which are guaranteed to be at least as long, cutting out every comparison against a word too short to ever contain it.

Observation 4: Tracing words equal to ["mass", "as", "hero", "superhero"] confirms it, once sorted by length, "as" is found inside "mass", "hero" is found inside "superhero", "mass" is checked against "superhero" but does not match, and "superhero" itself has nothing longer left to compare against at all, giving the correct final answer, ["as", "hero"], with far fewer wasted comparisons.
Recognizing that sorting by length first removes every comparison that could never succeed is what turns an all pairs, both directions search into a much smaller, one directional set of comparisons.
Compare every string against every other string in the array directly, checking whether one is a substring of the other.

items: For every string in the array, compare it against every other string.
If it is found as a substring of any other string, record it as a match.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every ordered pair of distinct indices is checked, so no possible substring relationship between two different words is ever missed.
The inner loop breaks immediately once a match is found for the current word, avoiding duplicate entries for the same qualifying word.
This checks both directions independently for every pair, since a substring relationship is not symmetric, one word containing the other does not imply the reverse.

blocks.text: Every pair of words is directly checked, so every genuine substring relationship in the array is correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(k squared times L squared) in the worst case, comparing every pair of the k words, each substring check costing up to O(L squared) with a naive comparison, where L is the maximum word length.
Space: O(k), for the result list.

Limitation: a shorter word can never be a substring of a word that is the same length or shorter, so many of these pairwise checks are guaranteed to fail before any character is even compared, and are worth skipping entirely.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it spends real comparison time on pairs that are mathematically guaranteed to fail, any pair where the "container" word is not strictly longer than the candidate.

What sorting by length fixes directly: once every word is ordered from shortest to longest, each word only ever needs to be checked against the words that come after it, which are guaranteed to be at least as long.

What is still needed on top of that: within those remaining, viable comparisons, an actual substring check is still required, since being longer does not guarantee containment.

The core idea: sort once by length, then only compare each word against strictly longer ones, cutting out every comparison that length alone already rules out.

Since a word can only ever be a substring of a strictly longer word, first sort all the words by length. Then, for each word, only check it against words that come later in this sorted order, which are guaranteed to be at least as long, cutting out every comparison against words that could never possibly contain it.
Sort by length first, then only compare each word against strictly longer (or equal length, then skip identical duplicates) words.

blocks.caption: Optimized: sort by length first, only checking each word against strictly longer ones

blocks.text: This works because sorting by length guarantees that every word appearing later in the order is at least as long as the current one, so restricting comparisons to only those later words never skips a genuine substring relationship, it only ever skips comparisons that were mathematically impossible to succeed in the first place.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(k log k) for the sort, plus O(k squared times L) for the remaining comparisons, a meaningful reduction in wasted comparisons versus checking every pair in both directions.
Space: O(k), for the sorted copy and the result list.

blocks.text: Sorting by a simple, cheap to compute property (length) before doing more expensive pairwise work (a substring search) is a common trick for pruning away comparisons that could never possibly succeed, without needing a more advanced data structure.

items: Comparing every word against every other word in both directions, doubling the work when only checking shorter words against longer ones is needed.
Forgetting to break out of the inner loop once a match is found, causing the same qualifying word to be added to the result more than once.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Duplicate words in the array","One copy is technically a substring of the identical other copy, depending on how the problem intends to handle exact duplicates."],["No word being a substring of any other","Correctly returns an empty list."]]}

blocks.text: Mention that for a very large number of very long strings, more advanced structures like a suffix automaton or the Aho-Corasick algorithm could reduce the substring checking cost further, though that level of machinery is well beyond what this problem, marked easy, actually calls for.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every pair in both directions", think: sort by length first, then only compare each word against strictly longer ones.
If the interviewer says "what if there are many very long strings", think: a suffix automaton or Aho-Corasick could reduce the substring search cost further, though it is likely overkill here.
If the interviewer says "what about duplicate words", think: clarify whether an exact duplicate should count as a substring of its identical twin before writing any code.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(k squared times L squared) time, O(k) space. Optimized: O(k log k) time for sorting plus O(k squared times L) time for the pruned comparisons, O(k) space.

items: Pattern: sort by length first, then only compare each word against strictly longer ones, pruning away comparisons that could never succeed.

Core Idea: a word can only ever be a substring of a strictly longer word, so sorting by length once and comparing only in that one direction removes every comparison that length alone already rules out.
Time: O(k squared times L squared) for the brute force, O(k log k) plus O(k squared times L) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(k) for both approaches.
Most Important Observation: sorting by a cheap, easily comparable property before expensive pairwise work is a general way to prune away guaranteed failures without needing new data structures.
Interview Difficulty: the length based pruning idea is simple and standard; recognizing it as an instance of a broader "sort first to prune impossible pairs" pattern shows extra depth.
One line memory trick: sort by length, then only ever check a word against something strictly longer.
